subject: ent
title: Maxillofacial fractures and CSF rhinorrhoea

steps.tx: Facial trauma triage protects airway from blood, swelling and displaced maxilla, plus cervical spine, eyes and brain before bones. **Zygomatic** fractures flatten cheek, restrict mouth opening through coronoid impingement, cause infraorbital **numbness** and diplopia from orbital floor involvement. Naso orbital ethmoid injuries telescope the nasal bridge with telecanthus. **Mandible** fractures malocclude, favour paired ring breaks, and threaten airway in bilateral parasymphyseal flail patterns.
steps.say: Triage starts with airway, spine, eyes and brain before any bone. Blood, swelling and a displaced maxilla block breathing quickly. Flat cheeks with numbness and trismus point toward zygomatic injury. Broken jaws disturb the bite and often break in two places. Bilateral front jaw breaks are dangerous because the tongue falls back.

steps.tx: Le Fort injuries separate the facial skeleton at levels, with type I low transverse above teeth giving floating **palate**, type II pyramidal through infraorbital rims with nasal bridge giving CSF risk, and type III craniofacial disjunction through arches with orbits giving floating **face**. All can bleed massively and block airway, mobile maxilla with malocclusion defines them, and CT with three dimensional planning restores **occlusion** first with buttress fixation.
steps.say: Le Fort patterns are the description of where the midface separates from the skull. Type one is a floating palate above the teeth. Type two is a floating nose pyramid with infraorbital steps. Type three is a floating face through the arches and orbits. All bleed heavily and threaten the airway. Repair restores the bite first with strong fixation, which is the priority.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram showing three types of Le Fort midface fractures: Le Fort I (horizontal), Le Fort II (pyramidal), and Le Fort III (craniofacial disjunction).
vis.caption: Le Fort midface fractures: I (transverse), II (pyramidal), III (craniofacial disjunction)

steps.tx: Orbital blowout fractures breach floor or medial wall into sinuses after blunt globe injury, trapping inferior rectus with diplopia worse on upgaze, later **enophthalmos**, infraorbital numbness and oculocardiac **bradycardia** in children with white eyed trapdoor urgency toward immediate release. Large defects with enophthalmos risk, muscle **entrapment** and retrobulbar haemorrhage with tense proptosed globe and vision loss needing lateral canthotomy complete the urgent list.
steps.say: Blowout fractures trap eye muscles after blunt injury, and double vision is the result. Double vision worse on looking up is a marker of inferior rectus entrapment. Children with white eyed trapdoor injuries need urgent release with heart slowing. Later sinking of the globe follows large defects. Tense proptosed eyes with vision loss mean compartment bleeding that needs canthotomy now.

steps.tx: This coronal CT shows a left orbital floor **blowout fracture** with herniated fat, teardrop sign, entrapped inferior rectus and maxillary fluid. The entrapped muscle explains diplopia worse on upgaze with nausea and **bradycardia** in children, marking white eyed **trapdoor** urgency. Treat entrapment with urgent release, and tense proptosed compartment blood with lateral canthotomy before vision dies.
steps.say: This scan is a display of the blowout fracture that traps eye muscle. Herniated fat with the teardrop sign hangs below the floor with fluid in the sinus, which is typical. The entrapped rectus explains double vision worse on looking up. Children with this trapdoor pattern need urgent release. Tense proptosed bleeding needs canthotomy before vision is lost.

vis.alt: Coronal CT showing left orbital floor blowout fracture with herniated fat, teardrop sign, entrapped inferior rectus and maxillary fluid
vis.caption: Coronal CT of orbital floor blowout fracture with entrapment. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Clear watery unilateral discharge after anterior skull base injury means **cerebrospinal fluid** leak until beta 2 transferrin says otherwise, worse leaning forward with salty taste and reservoir sign through cribriform, frontal or sphenoid fractures. Most traumatic leaks close within a week with head elevation and no straining or nose blowing, while persistent leaks, recurrent **meningitis** and large defects need endoscopic **repair**. Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent meningitis and generally stay withheld.
steps.say: Clear watery drip after head injury is spinal fluid until proven otherwise. Flow worsens leaning forward with a salty taste. Most traumatic leaks are sealed within a week with head elevation. Straining, blowing and nose picking are stopped during healing. Persistent leaks, meningitis or large defects are movers to endoscopic repair.
